summary: This informational RFC moves RFC 3627, which advised against using /127 prefixes between routers, to Historic status. RFC 6164 updates that guidance, and as a Standards Track document it takes precedence in conflicts.

eli5.summary: An old rule said not to do something. A newer rule says it is fine after all, so this marks the old rule as retired.

questions: ipv6 prefix length for router links
subtitle: Marks the old advice against /127 router links as Historic, so readers follow the newer RFC 6164 instead.

tldr.problem: RFC 3627 advised against /127 prefixes between routers, but RFC 6164 later gave updated guidance, and casual readers might not know which one to follow.
tldr.mechanism: This document moves RFC 3627 to Historic and obsoletes it, linking the two RFCs so that people reading the old one see it has been superseded.
tldr.outcome: A Standards Track document supersedes an informational one, so the guidance in RFC 6164 is to be followed where the two conflict.

today: RFC 6547 obsoletes RFC 3627 and moves it to Historic, and it updates RFC 6164, which holds the guidance to follow.

sections.title: Why a Link Was Needed
sections.content:
This document moves RFC 3627, "Use of /127 Prefix Length Between Routers Considered Harmful", to Historic status in accordance with RFC 2026. RFC 3627 has been superseded by RFC 6164, "Using 127-Bit IPv6 Prefixes on Inter-Router Links".

The two documents were not formally linked, which may not have been clear to casual readers unfamiliar with the differences in IETF document types.
sections.eli5: Two papers gave opposite advice, and nothing on the old one said it was out of date.

sections.title: Which Guidance Wins
sections.content:
The rule stated here is simple: a Standards Track document supersedes an informational document. Where RFC 6164 and RFC 3627 conflict, the guidance in RFC 6164 is to be followed.

This document adds the necessary link between the two RFCs, so that users who refer to RFC 3627 will see that it has been obsoleted by updated guidance. It also updates RFC 6164. It introduces no new security considerations.
sections.eli5: When a newer official rule and an older note disagree, you follow the official rule. This note makes that obvious.

sections.title: The Two RFCs Involved
sections.content: The text identifies RFC 3627 as published in September 2003 and RFC 6164 as published in April 2011. It does not restate the technical arguments of either document, so for the actual reasoning about prefix lengths on router links, read RFC 6164.
sections.eli5: This note does not explain the rule itself. It only says which paper to read.
